newsitem.title: GERMANY: Cotton set to stem loss of textile market share.
newsitem.headline: Cotton set to stem loss of textile market share.

text.p: Cotton will start to stem a loss of textile market share to synthetic fibres in the next few years, a U.S. cotton industry official said on Thursday.
"Beyond the year 2000, the loss of market share to man-made fibre (MMF) will see a slowdown," Mark Lange, director of economic services at the U.S. National Cotton Council (NCC), told Reuters.

Lange, speaking during a promotional tour of Europe, said cotton would benefit from income growth and growing quality awareness in fast-expanding Asian markets and from robust demand in key consumption centres.
MMF offered more security of cheap supply with crude oil prices set to fall. This explained why some less developed countries were expanding production capacity in synthetic fibres.
Cotton supply and prices, by contrast, could vary widely depending on the weather and other factors.

Cotton had lost about 0.6 percent of the world textile market to synthetics over the past two years and might lose another percent by 2000. But that would not be strongly felt in the U.S., Europe or highly developed Asian countries, which together accounted for 52.5 percent of world fibre consumption.
China and Pakistan operated a two-tier strategy, selling MMF products locally while exporting value-added cotton products.
Marsha Powell, European director of Cotton Council International, the NCC's export arm, said market research showed European consumers had a clear preference for cotton.
Lange said the price advantage enjoyed by synthetics remained the greatest challenge to cotton producers.

Latest MMF capacity expansion plans in Asia had been made in 1995, when cotton cost $2.53 per kilo and polyester $2.05. In 1997 textile companies had been paying an average $1.70 for cotton and $1.32 for polyester.
U.S. farmers had teamed up with government agencies to manage cotton pest control and were looking for yield rises and savings in production costs from transgenic seeds.
The NCC believed U.S. raw cotton production costs might be reduced by 10 to 18 percent over the next 10 years.
That, plus a sharp reduction in the use of chemicals, would boost consumer confidence in cotton in Europe and the U.S., Lange added.
Two million acres had been planted to transgenic cotton in the 1996/97 season out of total of 14.6 million in the U.S. Transgenic cotton's share might double in 1997/98.
